title: Chapter 2. When everything collapses: humanoids work for humans

blocks.text: There is a moment, in Pedro's idea, when the arrangement of the four coins can no longer hold. It is not a scene of rubble, nor a call to ruin. It is something more precise: the habit of renting out a life by the hour collapses. The custom of having to sell the day in order to deserve one's bread collapses. And, in that collapse, a figure appears that this century can no longer treat as a magazine drawing: the humanoid. A machine in the shape of a person, made to do what the human body has done for millennia in the workshop, the warehouse, the line, the house. Pedro's sentence says it in one stroke: “When everything collapses: humanoids work for humans.”

blocks.text: The preposition matters. They work for humans, not instead of leaving them without bread, and not over them. If the machines do the work and the fruit goes to whoever owns them, nothing will have collapsed: only the owner of the tool will have changed, and the four coins will go on measuring those who are no longer needed on the floor. This chapter holds to Pedro's idea and, at the same time, to the condition without which that idea would become a trap.

blocks.text: Once again, it is worth separating what already exists from what is still a horizon.
blocks.html: Once again, it is worth separating what already exists from what is still a horizon.

blocks.text: Humanoids have left the laboratory and begun to be tested in real factories, on concrete tasks, not in a science-fiction story. BMW Group has reported that, at its plant in Spartanburg, in the United States, Figure AI's Figure 02 robot took part in 2025, for some ten months, in the body shop, inserting sheet-metal parts for welding, and that it was involved in the production of more than 30,000 BMW X3 vehicles. In June 2026, the same company and Figure AI announced the next step: the Figure 03 model, intended for a logistics sequencing task, picking up components and sorting them into a cart for the line. Tesla, for its part, reported in 2026 that it had begun, at its factory in Fremont, California, production of the first production-quality units of its Optimus humanoid, and that it would continue to iterate the design and the process. None of that means that machines already work, in a general way, for human beings. It means that the gesture has begun: an artificial body, in a real workplace, does part of what a hired worker once did. The rest — scale, safety, usefulness for open-ended tasks, who benefits — remains to be seen. This book will not sell a catalogue. It will look at the possibility.

blocks.text: Because the possibility touches the nerve of chapter 1. If a day's work was valued at four coins, it was because a human body was needed to do the work. The wage, that way of renting out a life, was born of that need. When a machine can do what is repetitive, heavy, what wears out the back and asks for no vocation, the need to hire oneself out loses its blackmail. “Everything collapses” means that: the argument that there is no other way to organise bread falls away. It falls away, at least, in potential. What remains is to see that the fall does not leave the person underneath.

blocks.text: In the district of the Mar Menor this idea is not an abstraction from a technology fair. There has been fishing, market gardening, mining, the port, the season, the workshop. People who left home before dawn because the wage would not wait. If one day a humanoid loads, sorts, gathers or repairs what today steals the sun from those people, the question is not whether the machine “takes the job.” The question is whether the person gets the day back. A job lost, in the world of the four coins, is a threat. Work done by a machine, in the world Pedro imagines, would be a liberation: the heavy making is shifted, and what remains is the making we actually want — caring, teaching, deciding, cultivating for pleasure, being with others, looking at the lagoon. That liberation does not happen by itself. It happens if bread no longer depends on having kept the post.

blocks.text: There lies the danger, and it must be named without hedging and without pointing at anyone. Humanoids, today, are made by companies. The trials take place in plants that have owners. If the collapse of the old wage merely concentrates the gain in whoever owns the machine, we shall have repeated the history of the mine and the mint: the metal changes shape, the power does not. That is why this chapter does not close in the workshop. It opens towards those that follow. If humanoids truly work for humans, the fruit of that work has to reach the person in what they need — in the coupons of the next chapter — and cannot become the throne of a few. A just collapse does not leave human rubble. It leaves time.

blocks.text: Time is what the wage had priced. A clock, a payslip, a “see you tomorrow.” When the machine takes on the repeated hour, the clock can cease to be the master. Then an old question reappears, one that employment had covered over: what do we do with the day? It is not a small question. The void left by work that no longer rents us out can be filled with meaning or with hollow comfort. Later, this book will deal with that void. For now it is enough not to confuse the end of the rental with the end of the person. The humanoid works. The human lives. If that is reversed, if the human ends up serving the machine or whoever owns it, the title of this chapter will have been falsified.

blocks.text: Pedro does not ask that we stop making. He asks that we stop having to make in order to deserve to exist. The beloved craft — the baker who wants their bread, the person who tends a garden, who teaches, who repairs with pleasure, who accompanies — does not disappear because a machine knows how to lift a box. On the contrary: it can become a craft again, not a rental. What collapses is the obligation. What remains is chosen making, the kind that still looks you in the face.

blocks.text: From the shore, the scene can be imagined without ornament. Dawn comes up over the lagoon. The heavy work, somewhere, is being done by bodies that do not tire as a man or a woman tires. In the houses, there is time. That time is not guaranteed by the existence of the robot. It is guaranteed, if it is guaranteed, by the decision that the robot should be a common tool, or at least a tool whose fruit leaves no one out. Chapter 3 will speak of how what is necessary is then bought. Chapter 4, of what happens to the power of those who today have much. This chapter, for now, leaves the sentence in its place, with its promise and its condition:

blocks.text: When everything collapses — when the wage as the only passport to life falls away — humanoids can work for humans. It is not yet a fact of the world. It is the horizon of this book. And it is only worth it if, when the old arrangement comes down, the person is left standing, in charge of their day, and not out in the open, watching a machine work for someone else.

blocks.text: It can be objected that a machine does not care as a person cares, and that is true. That is why this chapter does not hand over to humanoids the work of care, or of teaching, or of conversation by the shore. It hands over what wearies without asking for a soul: the repetitive, the heavy, what is done today because there is no other choice. The rest remains human, or it would no longer deserve to be called life. A humanoid that worked for us would give us back precisely that remainder. A humanoid that did everything, even affection, would have taken it from us. The boundary is not technical. It is moral, and it must be drawn before the collapse leaves the house empty of people.

blocks.text: In the title, “everything collapses” may frighten. Catastrophe is not being celebrated here. What is being named is the end of an arrangement that can no longer hold: that of selling the day in order to deserve bread, when a machine can carry the hardest part of that day. If that end is steered with justice, what collapses is the blackmail, not dignity. If it is steered badly, both collapse. This book takes the first of those paths, and writes down the warning so as not to forget the second.

blocks.text: Nor is the point to sit and wait for a company to decide our fate. Today's trials are in particular factories, with particular owners, and it is as well that this should be known. Pedro's horizon asks for something more: that this artificial labour power be turned towards the common good, as a tool of everyone would be, not a new throne. In the meantime, the experiments should be watched with care and without enchantment. A sheet-metal part well placed by a robot is not yet the liberation of a district. It is, barely, the proof that the gesture is possible.
